title: The Three Days Kazuo Inamori Spent Refusing to Promise the Future
dek: In April 1961 eleven young employees demanded guarantees from Kyoto Ceramic, and its co-founder told them he could promise only how he would act.

story.event: Answering young employees who demanded guarantees about their future pay
story.summary: On 29 April 1961, eleven employees who had joined Kyoto Ceramic from high school the year before gave Kazuo Inamori a written demand for guaranteed pay rises and bonuses, threatening to resign together. Inamori said he could not promise the future but pledged that the company would benefit them; after three days of talks they withdrew the demand and stayed. He later said the episode changed the company's purpose from testing his technology to protecting employees' livelihoods, the basis of Kyocera's management rationale.
paragraphs: On 29 April 1961, Kazuo Inamori, then 29, was handed a written demand. It came from eleven young people who had joined Kyoto Ceramic straight from high school the year before. According to the company's archive, they wanted promises about their future, such as regular pay rises and bonuses, and said they would all resign if refused. The two-year-old firm was pushing to raise output; overtime had become routine, and staff were sometimes called in on Sundays.

Inamori knew how thin the ground was. He had started the company in Kyoto in 1959 with seven colleagues from his previous employer, on ¥3 million gathered by friends of his former boss, one of whom borrowed ¥10 million against his own house to keep it running. At first its only customer was Matsushita, and he later recalled a sense of urgency that losing those orders would bankrupt them. Even when business held up, he said, he could not shake the fear that the company might fail and cause its employees and shareholders great hardship. Until then, he told an interviewer in 2010, its purpose had been to test his own technology in the real world.

He would not promise what he could not see. "This is a new company so I can't make any promises about the future," he told them, in Kyocera's account, but he pledged to make sure the company benefited them and asked whether they could trust him that far. He also offered, by that account, to answer with his life if careless management ever cheated them. The talks lasted three days, moving in the end to his home. One by one the group came round; the last to hold out, their leader, took Inamori's hand and cried. They withdrew the demand and stayed.

Inamori later said he realised the young employees had been asking him to guarantee their livelihood, and that a company also exists to protect the livelihoods of its people. In 1967, soon after becoming president, he set down Kyocera's purpose as providing for the material and intellectual growth of all employees while contributing to society. In 2010, asked to rebuild the bankrupt Japan Airlines, he gave its staff the same purpose, though that rescue also cost many of them their jobs.

quote.text: Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus says the future can be met later with the same reason you use today. Inamori offered his young staff only that: his present conduct, not a guaranteed future. Yet afterwards he made their future the very thing he would worry about for the rest of his working life.

reflection: The eleven were not being unreasonable. They were working long overtime and some Sundays, and wanted to know their lives would hold. Inamori could not give them certainty, and he did not pretend to. What he offered was smaller and more honest: a statement of how he would act, and a willingness to be held to it.

People close to you may ask you for a guarantee one day, a family member wondering whether the risk is worth it, or a colleague deciding whether to join you. You do not owe them a forecast you cannot make. You can owe them a clear account of what you will do, and the patience to keep talking until they believe it.
invitation: Think of one person whose plans depend a little on yours. Write one sentence you could honestly promise them, about how you will act rather than how things will turn out, and keep it where you will see it.

sources.title: Kyocera's Management Philosophy is established after contentious demands of young employees are successfully resolved (1961)
sources.publisher: Kazuo Inamori Archive, Official Site of Kazuo Inamori (Kyocera Corporation)
sources.supports: Date of 29 April 1961; eleven high school graduates hired the previous year; written demand for promises such as regular raises and bonuses, with a threat that all would resign; routine overtime and Sunday work; Inamori's replies, including 'This is a new company so I can't make any promises about the future' and 'If you feel cheated by my sloppy management, go ahead and stab me to death'; three days of talks ending at his home; the leader taking his hand and crying; in 1967, after becoming president, the philosophy of the material and intellectual well-being of all employees and contribution to society.

sources.title: 2F Technology and Management: Exhibition Details (Kyocera Corporation: Created the management rationale)
sources.publisher: Inamori Library, Official Site of Kazuo Inamori (Kyocera Corporation)
sources.supports: Founding of Kyoto Ceramic in April 1959 with seven colleagues; original purpose to present Inamori's technology to the world; new employees hired the previous year demanding wage guarantees early in the company's third year; three days and nights of talks; the employees withdrawing their demands and remaining with the company; the opening line of the management rationale.

sources.title: Oral history interview with Kazuo Inamori (interviewed by Thomas R. Tritton, Kyoto, 19 April and 13 November 2010)
sources.supports: Inamori's own account (through an interpreter): founded in 1959 with seven colleagues; ¥3 million in starting capital collected by friends of his former boss Masaji Aoyama, one of whom borrowed ¥10 million against his house for the company; Matsushita (Panasonic) as the only first customer and his urgency that losing it would mean bankruptcy; the 1961 episode in which young employees asked him to guarantee their livelihood; the earlier purpose of testing Kazuo Inamori's technology; his realisation that a company exists to protect employees' livelihoods; the management rationale wording; his 2010 chairmanship of Japan Airlines.

sources.title: YuYu interview, Kazuo Inamori
sources.supports: Founding with three million yen in capital and support from others; worrying every day that the company might fail, and the fear, even as business went well, that it might go out of business and cause employees and shareholders great hardship; the management rationale 'To provide opportunities for the material and intellectual growth of all our employees'.

sources.title: Why Is a Philosophy Needed in Management? (Origin of the Kyocera Philosophy)
sources.supports: Inamori's initial goal of showcasing his technology; collective bargaining by young employees seeking job security early in the company's third year, after a photo taken on 1 April 1961; the resulting purpose of the material and intellectual growth of all employees; his determination that the company must not fail; the 1967 management policy announced shortly after he became president.

sources.title: Kyocera founder Kazuo Inamori dead at 90
sources.supports: Inamori became chairman of the bankrupt Japan Airlines in 2010 and told employees its purpose was the material and intellectual growth of all employees; a large percentage of JAL employees were made redundant during the restructuring.

sources.title: Creating a setting for 'great leaps' of the imagination
sources.supports: Inamori founded Kyocera in April 1959, aged 26 to 27, with seven subordinates from his previous company and backing from older supporters.

The episode changed the company's stated purpose from testing Inamori's technology to protecting employees' livelihoods and well-being
Kyocera's management rationale is to provide opportunities for the material and intellectual growth of all employees
Inamori founded the company in 1959 with seven colleagues from his previous employer

research_notes: The detailed account of the 1961 talks (the date of 29 April, eleven employees, the threat of mass resignation, three days ending at Inamori's home, the leader's tears, and Inamori's two quoted replies) comes only from Kyocera's own archive; the story attributes it to that account. Inamori's own words in the 2010 Science History Institute oral history (spoken in Japanese, rendered by an interpreter) independently confirm that young employees asked him to guarantee their livelihood in 1961 and that this changed the company's purpose. Headcount: Kyocera's archive says 11; a search summary of Inamori's 2015 Ritsumeikan University lecture gives 'around ten', but that PDF could not be loaded for checking, so the story uses Kyocera's 11. Dating of the philosophy: Kyocera's chronology lists the management rationale as established in 1961, while its episode page and philosophy page say Inamori defined the management philosophy in 1967 after becoming president; the story says the episode changed his view in 1961 and that he set the purpose down in 1967. The wording of the rationale varies slightly across Kyocera pages ('well-being' or 'growth'); the story paraphrases it. Founding money: the oral history says friends of Aoyama gathered ¥3 million and one borrowed ¥10 million against his house; the Christian Science Monitor (1982) says friends put up money while Inamori's group contributed technology. Funding is therefore marked 'mixed' (private backers plus a loan). The CSM gives his age at founding as 26 (he turned 27 in January 1959). The JAL redundancies are from Asia Times and are mentioned so as not to overstate the rationale's record. Inamori's quoted line about being 'stabbed to death' is Kyocera's English translation of his words. Editor: Inamori's literal words in Kyocera's English translation ("go ahead and stab me to death") are paraphrased in the story for a gentler morning read; the meaning is unchanged.
